item.title: Downside-Only Risk and Risk per Unit of Return
item.summary: Standard deviation treats upside and downside surprises alike and says nothing about how large the risk is relative to the average return. Semi-deviation isolates the below-average (or below-target) side of the spread, and the coefficient of variation scales risk by the mean so that different investments can be compared on one footing.

sections.heading: Why plain standard deviation is not enough
sections.body_markdown: Standard deviation measures how far returns typically wander from their average, in both directions. A **return** is the percentage gain or loss on an investment over a period. Most investors are happy when a return lands far *above* average and unhappy only when it lands far *below*. Think of a commute: arriving 20 minutes early and arriving 20 minutes late both count as a deviation from the usual 40 minutes, but only the late arrival hurts. Standard deviation cannot tell those two apart, so analysts add a measure that looks at the unwelcome side only.

sections.heading: Semi-deviation: spread of the bad side only
sections.body_markdown:
**Semi-deviation** (also called semideviation) is a standard-deviation-style measure that uses only observations *below the mean*. Steps: (1) compute the mean $\bar X$; (2) keep only the observations lower than $\bar X$; (3) square each of their distances from the mean and add them up; (4) divide by $n-1$, where $n$ is the **total** number of observations, not just the number kept; (5) take the square root.

Because only some squared deviations enter the numerator while the denominator is unchanged, semi-deviation can never exceed the sample standard deviation computed from the same data. A variant, **target semi-deviation**, replaces the mean with a chosen target return $B$ (for example, a minimum acceptable return) and uses only the observations below $B$. This fits an investor who cares about falling short of a specific goal.

sections.heading: Coefficient of variation: risk per unit of return
sections.body_markdown:
A standard deviation of 10 points means something very different for an asset averaging 4% than for one averaging 20%. The **coefficient of variation (CV)** divides the standard deviation by the mean, so it expresses risk as a fraction (or percentage) of the average:

$$CV=\frac{s}{\bar X}$$

For returns, CV reads as the amount of risk taken per unit of average return, so a *lower* CV is better. It lets you compare investments whose averages differ widely. Its weakness is the denominator: when the mean is close to zero the CV explodes, and when the mean is negative the ratio is hard to interpret, so it is unreliable in those cases.

sections.heading: Putting the two together on an exam
sections.body_markdown: Expect to be asked to (a) compute semi-deviation or target semi-deviation by hand from a short list of returns, remembering the $n-1$ denominator, (b) compute and compare CVs for two assets, and (c) explain what each measure adds beyond standard deviation. Semi-deviation answers 'how bad are the bad outcomes?'; CV answers 'how much risk per unit of average return?'. Neither replaces standard deviation; both are used alongside it.

worked_example.problem: A fund had annual returns of 10%, 2%, -6%, 8% and 6% over five years. Treat these as a sample. Calculate (a) the mean, (b) the semi-deviation relative to the mean, (c) the sample standard deviation and (d) the coefficient of variation.
steps: Deviations from the mean: 6, -2, -10, 4, 2 (in percentage points).
Semi-deviation keeps only observations below 4%: these are 2% (deviation -2) and -6% (deviation -10).
Divide by n - 1 = 4 (all five observations count in n, not just the two kept): 104 / 4 = 26.

Sample standard deviation: squared deviations are 36 + 4 + 100 + 16 + 4 = 160; 160 / 4 = 40; square root = 6.32%. BA II Plus: 2nd [DATA], 2nd [CLR WORK], then enter 10 ENTER ↓ ↓ 2 ENTER ↓ ↓ -6 ENTER ↓ ↓ 8 ENTER ↓ ↓ 6 ENTER; then 2nd [STAT], press 2nd [SET] until 1-V appears, and scroll ↓ to read X̄ = 4 and Sx = 6.3246. (The calculator does not give semi-deviation, so step 6 is done by hand.)
CV = standard deviation / mean = 6.3246 / 4 = 1.58. Semi-deviation (5.10%) is below the standard deviation (6.32%), as it must be.
worked_example.answer: Mean = 4%; semi-deviation ≈ 5.10%; sample standard deviation ≈ 6.32%; CV ≈ 1.58 (about 1.58 units of risk per unit of average return).

formulas.name: Semi-deviation (below the mean)
formulas.where: X_i is each observation, \bar X is the sample mean, the sum includes only observations below the mean, and n is the total number of observations in the sample.

formulas.name: Target semi-deviation
formulas.where: B is the chosen target return, X_i is each observation, the sum includes only observations below B, and n is the total number of observations.

formulas.name: Coefficient of variation
formulas.where: s is the standard deviation of the data and \bar X is the mean; the result is a unitless ratio (multiply by 100 for a percentage).

exam_traps: Dividing the below-mean squared deviations by the number of below-mean observations (or that number minus one) instead of n - 1 using all observations.
Including observations that are above the mean (or above the target) in the semi-deviation sum.
Reading a higher CV as better: for returns, a lower CV means less risk per unit of return.
Choosing the investment with the lower standard deviation when the means differ, instead of comparing CVs.
Trusting a CV when the mean return is near zero or negative, where the ratio is unstable or hard to interpret.
leads_to: Downside risk measures such as target shortfall

issues: error found: CV and standard deviation parts are supported. The worked example has an error: semi-deviation of sqrt(26)=5.10% is below SD 6.32%, which is fine, but the claim that semi-deviation can never exceed standard deviation is true only here because both use n-1 over a subset of deviations. The statement is correct, so the real problem is elsewhere. The BA II Plus steps are plausible. All arithmetic checks: mean 4, 104/4=26, sqrt=5.10, 160/4=40, sqrt=6.32, CV=1.58. No error found on re-check, but the flag is set in error: error_found should be false.

item.stem: An analyst computes the sample standard deviation and the semi-deviation (relative to the mean) from the same series of annual returns. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Semi-deviation is larger because it focuses on the worst outcomes only.
options.explanation: Wrong: this assumes using fewer observations makes the result bigger. The denominator stays n - 1 while the numerator drops terms, so semi-deviation gets smaller.

options.text: Semi-deviation is never larger than the standard deviation, because it uses only some of the squared deviations.
options.explanation: Correct: both use the same n - 1 denominator, but semi-deviation sums only the below-mean squared deviations, so it cannot exceed the standard deviation.

options.text: The two are equal whenever the return distribution is symmetric.
options.explanation: Wrong: symmetry means about half the squared deviations fall below the mean, so the semi-deviation is roughly 70% of the standard deviation, not equal to it.

item.stem: A sample of returns has a mean of 5% and a standard deviation of 8%. What is the coefficient of variation? Round to two decimals.

options.explanation: Correct: CV = standard deviation / mean = 8 / 5 = 1.60.
Wrong: this inverts the ratio (mean / standard deviation = 5 / 8).
Wrong: this divides the variance (64, in squared percentage points) by the mean instead of the standard deviation.

item.stem: A sample of five annual returns is 9%, -3%, 5%, 1% and 3%. Calculate the semi-deviation relative to the mean using the sample (n - 1) convention. Round to two decimals.

options.explanation: Wrong: the sum of squared below-mean deviations (40) was divided by 2, the number of below-mean observations, instead of n - 1 = 4.
Wrong: the sum (40) was divided by n = 5 rather than n - 1 = 4.
Correct: the mean is 3%. Below-mean observations are -3% (deviation -6) and 1% (deviation -2). Squares: 36 + 4 = 40. Divide by 4 to get 10; the square root is 3.16%.

item.stem: Fund A has a mean annual return of 8% and a standard deviation of 12%. Fund B has a mean annual return of 12% and a standard deviation of 15%. Which conclusion about risk per unit of return is correct?

options.text: Fund A has less risk per unit of return because its standard deviation is lower.
options.explanation: Wrong: this compares raw standard deviations and ignores that the two funds have different mean returns.

options.text: Fund A has less risk per unit of return because its higher CV means more return per unit of risk.
options.explanation: Wrong: this misreads the CV. A higher CV (1.50 for A) means more risk per unit of return, which is worse.

options.text: Fund B has less risk per unit of return because its CV of 1.25 is below Fund A's CV of 1.50.
options.explanation: Correct: CV for A = 12/8 = 1.50 and for B = 15/12 = 1.25. The lower CV means less risk per unit of average return.

item.stem: Which statement describes a limitation of using the coefficient of variation to evaluate investment returns?

options.text: It becomes unstable or hard to interpret when the mean return is close to zero or negative.
options.explanation: Correct: the mean is the denominator, so a tiny mean makes the CV huge and a negative mean makes the ratio hard to interpret.

options.text: It ignores dispersion because it is calculated from the mean alone.
options.explanation: Wrong: the numerator is the standard deviation, so dispersion is the core of the measure.

options.text: It can be computed only for populations, not for samples.
options.explanation: Wrong: the sample version uses the sample standard deviation divided by the sample mean.

item.stem: An investor has a minimum acceptable return of 5%. Five annual returns were 7%, 3%, -1%, 5% and 2%. Calculate the target semi-deviation relative to 5% using the sample (n - 1) convention, counting only returns below the target. Round to two decimals.

options.explanation: Wrong: the sum of squared shortfalls (49) was divided by 3, the number of observations below the target, instead of n - 1 = 4.
Correct: returns below 5% are 3, -1 and 2, with shortfalls -2, -6 and -3. Squares: 4 + 36 + 9 = 49. Divide by 4 to get 12.25; the square root is 3.50%.
Wrong: the sum (49) was divided by n = 5 rather than n - 1 = 4.

item.stem: Two assets have very different average returns. Why might an analyst prefer the coefficient of variation to the standard deviation when comparing their risk?

options.text: The CV captures only downside variation and ignores returns above the mean.
options.explanation: Wrong: this describes semi-deviation. The CV uses the full standard deviation, upside included.

options.text: The CV converts the standard deviation into the probability of losing money.
options.explanation: Wrong: the CV is a ratio of standard deviation to mean. It is not a probability.

options.text: The CV expresses risk per unit of average return, putting the two assets on a common scale.
options.explanation: Correct: dividing by the mean adjusts for scale, so assets with different average returns can be compared directly.

item.front: How is semi-deviation (relative to the mean) calculated, and what is its denominator?
item.back: Square the deviations of only the below-mean observations, add them, divide by n - 1 (n = ALL observations), then take the square root.

item.front: What does target semi-deviation measure, and how does it differ from ordinary semi-deviation?
item.back: It measures dispersion of returns falling below a chosen target B (such as a minimum acceptable return), using shortfalls from B instead of deviations from the mean.

item.front: What is the coefficient of variation and how do you read it for returns?
item.back: CV = standard deviation / mean. It is risk per unit of average return, so a lower CV is better. It is unreliable when the mean is near zero or negative.

item.front: How does semi-deviation compare in size with the sample standard deviation of the same data?
item.back: It is never larger, because it sums only some of the squared deviations but uses the same n - 1 denominator.

warnings: 2/7 items have the longest option as the key
